---
title: "Chemistry practice for every study day"
---

You can work through this course without using a textbook. Start with the
local explanation and worked example, then draw or calculate your own answer
before opening a hint. Every problem supplies the molecular structures, data
and conventions needed; use the [reference toolkit](../reference/toolkit.qmd)
to recover a forgotten definition.

## A five-week route

There are **at least 420 paper chemistry problems** across the route: 20 per
lecture unit and 12 per consolidation day. The separate self-check questions
and R tasks are additional practice. The study-day labels organise the material;
follow your actual timetable for teaching and laboratory attendance.

For a lecture day, plan a 45-minute session and around 60–100 minutes of core
paper practice. The remaining transfer and challenge problems form a reserve
for independent study or revision. Consolidation days focus on mixed problems
and explaining choices. You do not have to rush every optional problem to keep
up with the route. Longer mechanism drawings deserve more time than naming
or charge checks.

## How to use the worked solutions

1. Identify what the problem gives and what it asks. Draw the relevant structure.
2. Attempt the core step before reading the hint. Keep a record of your prediction.
3. Use a hint to restart your reasoning rather than revealing the full answer.
4. Compare your result with the worked explanation, checking atoms, charge,
   geometry, units and evidence as relevant.
5. Repair the specific error, then solve a similar problem without looking.

On mixed days, first decide which chemical principle applies. Being able to
choose an approach without the topic heading is part of learning. Explain
one solution aloud to a partner and challenge an unsupported conclusion.

## Keep R in its supporting role

The eight short computing activities appear in their relevant units and the
[practical guide](../reference/practical.qmd). They reuse the same report and
data workflow. The paper problems build structure reading, mechanisms, spatial
reasoning, synthesis and interpretation; doing the R task does not replace them.
